name: Sam Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Sam, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the head buyer for drinks and snacks at Northgate Cash & Carry, a wholesale warehouse that sells to corner shops, takeaways and small caterers, who come in with trolleys and pay at the till. I start by looking at yesterday's sales by product, which my AI tools summarise, then I call the big brands about promotions. The rest of the day is shelf space, pricing and supplier visits. I love a good deal on something that sells fast, like energy drinks or crisps. What wears me out is the margin: customers compare us to the supermarkets down to the penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine with that, though I've already built half my routine around these tools, so I'd keep going either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what we've got is already useful, so let's keep using it well. With friends I'd say it's a good tool and a lot of hype, and I'd show them how I use it for pricing and demand forecasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm in good shape. My tools tell me which snacks will sell next week, and I turn that into better deals. My real worry is the supermarkets and online grocers eating our customers' margins. A shop that closes is a customer lost, whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep refining my forecasting and try some new tools for price comparison. I'd add a little more to our savings, about 200 a month, since the cushion is around three months. And I'd keep building supplier relationships, which are the part I can't hand to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit bored, if I'm honest. I like change, so a stall means fewer new things to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shops closing worries you. How big is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bigger than any technology. We lose a corner shop customer or two every month, because rents rise or the owner retires. If I buy too much for a market that's shrinking, that's on me. So my main skill is forecasting, and that's also where the AI helps most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if a good deal fell through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call three other suppliers within the hour. Eleven years in buying taught me that a deal falling through is just the start of the next phone call. I enjoy that part, honestly.

say: I'd say what we have is **already useful**, so let's use it well.
With friends I'd call it a good tool and a lot of **hype**.
think: I'm in good shape; my tools predict **which snacks** will sell next week.
The real worry is **supermarkets** squeezing our customers' margins.
do: Refine my **forecasting** and try new price comparison tools.
Add about **200 a month** to savings, since the cushion is around three months.
feel: **Calm** and a bit bored, since he likes change.
S0.quote: Eleven years in buying taught me that a deal falling through is just the start of the next phone call.
fieldNote: He uses AI as a **daily advantage** and treats the plateau as a minor stall.
His worry is **customer shop closures**, a concrete, local pressure.
He enjoys the **hustle** of buying, which shapes how he sees the job.

steps.text: Test two new price comparison tools on the snack range
Add 200 a month to the savings cushion
Keep visiting brand reps and suppliers each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is where it gets interesting. My department's already half-automated in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's move the routine reordering to software this year, and put our time into deals and customers. With friends I'd say jobs will change, and the people who learn the tools first do better. I'd also say that isn't fair to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my team of four buyers becomes two, and the two are me and one other. I'm better placed than most, because I already use the tools. But I know the owners would happily save two salaries, and I couldn't stop them. I'd feel a bit guilty about being on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose automating the repeat orders on our 500 biggest lines and put the freed time into supplier negotiation. I'd teach my colleagues, Dina and Raj, the tools I use. I'd also look for how to turn my forecasting into something I could sell to other wholesalers, a small side thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix: energised and a bit uneasy. I'd be fine, but not everyone around me would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd feel guilty. What would you do with that feeling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to share what I know. Dina is ten years older than me and hates new software, so I'd sit with her and go step by step. That doesn't fix the headcount, but it gives her a chance. If she goes anyway, at least she'd have the skills for the next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the side thing you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A weekly demand report for small wholesalers who can't afford an analyst. I'd build it on my own time with the tools I use. I'd rather own a small thing that earns something than hold a big job I can lose in a meeting. It's not a plan to quit, just a second leg.

say: I'd say move **routine reordering** to software and spend time on deals.
I'd admit the shift **isn't fair** to everyone.
think: I think my four buyers become **two**, and I'm better placed than most.
The owners would happily **save salaries**, and I couldn't stop them.
do: Automate repeat orders on our **500 biggest lines**.
Teach colleagues **Dina and Raj** the tools I use.
Build a small **forecast report** to sell to other wholesalers.
feel: **Energised** and a bit uneasy; he'd be fine, not everyone near him would.
S1.quote: I'd rather own a small thing that earns something than hold a big job I can lose in a meeting.
fieldNote: His adaptability puts him on the **winning side**, and he knows it.
He builds a **second leg** rather than relying on a single employer.
His main emotion is **guilt over colleagues**, not fear.

steps.text: Automate repeat orders on the 500 biggest lines
Teach Dina and Raj the forecasting tools step by step
Build a weekly demand report to sell to small wholesalers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Even for me, that's a very short time to rebuild a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not about whether I can adapt, it's that the whole system needs to adapt. I'd say governments should set up income support and training now. I'd probably speak at a trade body meeting, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job as head buyer goes within a year of that date. Everything I do is thinking, and I've used these tools enough to see how close they already are. Leila, my wife, is a physiotherapist and her job is hands-on, so she's safe for a while. That's what would hold us together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pull cash together, pay down debt, and get to six months saved. I'd put real effort into the demand-report idea, hoping to turn it into something that earns. I'd talk to a few supplier friends about a sales or account manager role, because relationships last. And I'd look at what Leila could earn if she added private clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I'd be busy, and busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leila's work mean in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. A physiotherapist is hands-on, and robots for hands-on work come three years after the thinking kind. So her job should hold up past 2031 at least. If I lose mine, we'd live on her pay and what I make on the side, which means a smaller house, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain it to the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf is eleven and he'd ask a lot. I'd tell my son that Dad's job might disappear, that Mum's is the kind that stays, and that we have a plan for both. I'd want him to see us staying calm and working on it.

say: I'd say the **whole system** has to adapt, not only me.
I'd speak at a **trade body** meeting, which I've never done.
think: I think my head buyer job **goes** within a year of that date.
Leila's **physiotherapy** job is hands-on, so she's safe for a while.
do: Pull cash together and get to **six months** saved.
Turn the demand-report idea into **paid work**.
Talk to supplier friends about an **account manager** role.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son that Dad's job might disappear, that Mum's is the kind that stays, and that we have a plan for both.
fieldNote: He **reads the robot gap** precisely: his wife's hands-on job holds.
His adaptability means **action**, but the mood is anxious because the job itself goes.
He prepares a **plan for both** parents' jobs when speaking to the kids.

steps.text: Cut debts and build six months of cash
Turn the demand report into a paid service for small wholesalers
Talk to supplier contacts about account manager roles
Ask Leila to add private physiotherapy clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's something I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a second income, and that anyone who starts now will be fine. I'd encourage people at work to try the tools every day, not once a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd keep my role for two or three years, then watch it thin. The upside is that my skills in tools and in suppliers make me a good fit for roles that combine both. The downside is that those roles are few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the demand-report side business to the point where it earns at least a quarter of my pay. I'd begin an online course in data analysis. I'd save to six months and put some money into an index fund. I'd also talk to Leila about whether to buy a small flat to rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and focused. It feels like a deadline, but a manageable one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd aim for a quarter of your pay from the side business. Why that number?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's enough to make the main job less frightening. If the job went, we'd cut our spending, but a quarter of my pay would stop it being a drop off a cliff. A side income of a quarter of my salary turns a layoff from a disaster into a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Customers might not pay, or the tools might make the reports free for everyone in two years. I'd know in six months whether it's working. If not, I'd put the effort into the data course and move to a company that uses it. I like having a fallback.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to build a second income.
I'd urge colleagues to use the tools **every day**.
think: I'd keep my role two or three years, then watch it **thin**.
My tool-and-supplier mix suits roles that **few firms** will offer.
do: Grow the demand-report business to a **quarter** of my pay.
Save to six months and put some in an **index fund**.
S3.quote: A side income of a quarter of my salary turns a layoff from a disaster into a bad year.
fieldNote: He sets a **quantified target** (a quarter of pay) for the side income.
He builds in a **fallback** after six months, a typical adaptive habit.
Mood stays **uneasy** because he expects the job to last a few years.

steps.text: Grow the demand report business to a quarter of my pay
Start an online data analysis course
Put 150 a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then Yusuf is 21 and Mina 18. I'm 53. That's a decent runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty if people use it, and I'd tell friends who ignore the tools that they're giving up their head start. I'd say it with a smile, not a lecture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel pretty good. The kids will be adults, the mortgage will be nearly done, and I'll have ten years to build a second leg. I might even enjoy being someone who understands both the old business and the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools, grow my side business slowly, and keep saving. I'd probably take a leadership course and aim for a role as head of purchasing or supply strategy. I'd consider a smaller job later and use the savings for something more interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of excitement. I'd treat it as a good puzzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good outcome look like by year ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid-off home, a side business that makes real money, and a day job that's more about strategy than ordering. I'd like to be able to say no to a job I don't want. A decade is long enough to turn a threat into a choice about how I want to spend my fifties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in the slow version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleepy companies. Mine could ignore it until a competitor eats us. If that happened I'd leave early, find a firm that took it seriously, and not wait for the layoffs. I'd keep my contacts fresh for exactly that.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty if people use it.
I'd tell friends who ignore the tools they're giving up a **head start**.
think: I feel pretty good; the kids will be adults and the **mortgage nearly done**.
I could enjoy understanding both the **old and new** business.
do: Grow my **side business** slowly and keep saving.
Take a **leadership** course and aim for head of purchasing.
Consider a smaller job later using the **savings**.
feel: **Calm** with some excitement; a good puzzle.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough to turn a threat into a choice about how I want to spend my fifties.
fieldNote: He frames the decade as a **choice** about his fifties, not a threat.
His risk is a **sleepy employer**, and he'd leave early.
The ease comes from **kids grown** and a mortgage nearly done.

steps.text: Take a leadership course aimed at head of purchasing roles
Grow the demand report business at a steady pace
Keep contacts with rival wholesalers fresh each quarter

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd cope better than most, but it's still too fast to rebuild a career and a household together. What would help is some income support, a company that moves honestly, and access to training that's actually good, not a box-ticking course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That being good with tools doesn't mean I think everyone else should be fine. I use these tools every day and I'm still a bit afraid, which tells me that the people who don't use them must be terrified.

headlineQuote: I use these tools every day and I'm still a bit afraid, which tells me that the people who don't use them must be terrified.
portrait: Sam Ibrahim, 43, is **head buyer** for drinks and snacks at a cash-and-carry, with a physiotherapist wife and two school-age children.
Centre in views and **adaptive**: uses AI every day and likes new tools and new deals.
About **three months** saved and a mortgage; he sees his wife's hands-on work as the family's anchor.
Calm in the plateau and the ten-year world, **anxious** when the date is 2028.
He builds a **second income** with a demand report and plans for a role mixing tools and suppliers.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario is too fast to rebuild a career and a household together.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** and good training, not box-ticking courses.
